title: Links Golf vs Parkland Golf: Two Completely Different Games
summary: Many golfers spend their lives playing parkland courses without ever truly understanding links golf. The two formats demand different skills, different thinking, and a completely different relationship with the wind.
content:
Golf is not one game. It is at least two, and arguably more. The game played on a parkland course — manicured fairways, defined rough, predictable bounces, little wind influence — is a game of precision. Control the ball through the air. Land it on the target. Manage the distance. The game played on a links course is something else entirely: a game of imagination, of adaptation, of making peace with unpredictability and finding ways to score despite it.

Most professional golfers have learned both. Many amateur golfers, particularly those who play predominantly on parkland or parkland-influenced courses, have never truly learned links golf. They arrive at a traditional links — in Scotland, in Ireland, on England's coastline — and find that the skills they have spent years refining are suddenly inadequate. The wind does things they did not anticipate. The ball bounces in directions they did not expect. The greens run at speeds and angles that parkland golf never required them to manage.

What Makes a Links Course

Links land is coastal, sandy ground, typically found between the sea and the more fertile inland terrain where farming was possible. The word links itself refers to this type of terrain. The courses that developed on it — St Andrews, Royal Birkdale, Carnoustie, Royal Portrush — share characteristics that follow from the landscape rather than from design choices. The turf is firm and fast. The fairways are often undulating in ways that parkland architects would consider too severe. The rough is genuine rough — fescue grasses that grip the ball and punish offline shots. And there are almost always bunkers placed where the prevailing winds tend to push the ball.

Most importantly, there is the wind. On a links course in a full coastal gale, golf becomes a genuinely different test. A shot that would travel 170 yards in still air might travel 200 yards downwind or 140 yards into the wind. The same 7-iron becomes a 5-iron or a 9-iron depending on what the wind is doing, and the wind can change between the time you club up and the time you hit the ball.

The Ground Game

The defining tactical difference between links and parkland is the ground game. On a parkland course, the ideal shot lands on the target, checks with backspin, and stops near the flag. The ball's interaction with the ground is an endpoint rather than a tool. On a links course, the ground is a tool. Players who understand links golf learn to use the turf — to run the ball along the ground to the pin when hitting through the air would expose the shot to too much wind, to bump-and-run from the apron rather than chipping through the air, to read the slope and contour of the approach and use them rather than fight them.

This requires a different set of shots and a different mental approach. The golfer who insists on aerial precision at a links course will score worse than the golfer who adapts. The wind does not respect the ability to control ball flight. The player who accepts this and finds ways to use the ground scores well. The player who fights against the conditions scores poorly and probably has a miserable time.

When you first play links golf properly — when you really commit to the ground game, to running the ball, to trusting the bounce — something clicks. You realise there are so many more options than you thought. The game opens up. It is a completely different kind of creativity.

Why The Open Championship Matters

The Open Championship is played exclusively on links courses, which is why it identifies a different kind of champion than the other three majors. Augusta National, a parkland course of exceptional precision, rewards a different skill set than Carnoustie. Oakmont or Bethpage, US Open venues, demand the ability to manage severe rough and undulating greens. But a links major tests the ability to adapt — to manage the weather, to use the ground, to think creatively under conditions that change from hour to hour.

Many great players have won multiple majors but struggled to win The Open. The reverse is also true: players from links-golf traditions — Scots, Irish, Northern English — have historically been disproportionately successful at Open venues. The game they grew up playing, the creativity and adaptability links conditions demanded, translated directly into major championship performance. The two games are related but distinct, and mastering both is one of professional golf's most rewarding challenges.
